what_it_does: Fades dark spots by reducing melanin production in the skin.
summary_short: Hydroquinone is one of the most effective topical ingredients for stubborn hyperpigmentation, including melasma and dark spots. It works best under professional guidance because overuse can irritate skin and, rarely, cause paradoxical darkening.
summary_long:
Hydroquinone is a pigment-fading ingredient used for concerns like melasma, sun spots, and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. It works mainly by inhibiting tyrosinase, an enzyme involved in melanin production, which helps reduce excess pigment over time rather than bleaching skin instantly.

It has stronger clinical support than many cosmetic brighteners, but it is also more treatment-like than routine skincare. Results usually take several weeks to months and depend heavily on consistent sunscreen use; ongoing UV exposure can quickly undo progress or worsen discoloration.

Common strengths vary by country and product type. In places where it is available by prescription, 4% hydroquinone is a common dermatology strength, while lower strengths have historically appeared in over-the-counter products in some markets. It is often used in short cycles rather than indefinitely.

The main downsides are irritation, dryness, stinging, redness, and increased sensitivity, especially when combined with exfoliating acids or retinoids. A rare but important risk with prolonged or improper use is exogenous ochronosis, a blue-gray or dark discoloration that can be difficult to treat; this is one reason many dermatologists recommend supervised, time-limited use.

Hydroquinone is often paired with sunscreen, retinoids, azelaic acid, kojic acid, vitamin C, or prescription anti-inflammatory ingredients depending on the case. Avoid layering it casually with multiple strong actives unless directed, and do not use it on broken or irritated skin.
quick_facts: Strong option for stubborn dark spots
Often used in short treatment cycles
